Read the transcript of the audio guide
  1. As a girl in Havana, Celia Cruz earned her first pair of shoes by singing for a tourist. source
  2. Fifty years later she gave her stage shoes to the Smithsonian. source
  3. She was born in Havana on 21 October 1925, into a poor family. source
  4. According to the Smithsonian, she was one of fourteen children, and her singing began at home. source
  5. That voice soon reached bigger audiences. source
  6. She went on to sing with the Cuban band La Sonora Matancera. source
  7. Soon after Fidel Castro took power in 1959, Cruz was touring in Mexico with La Sonora Matancera. source
  8. She did not go home. source
  9. Most accounts date her departure to 1960 and her move to the United States to 1961. source
  10. According to her biographers, Castro's government barred her from returning to Cuba. source
  11. She made her life in New York and New Jersey, and sang about Cuba for the rest of her career. source
  12. She recorded and performed with musicians such as Tito Puente and Johnny Pacheco. source
  13. On 14 October 1994, on the South Lawn of the White House, President Clinton presented the National Medal of Arts. source
  14. He said: source
  15. Celia Cruz has used her powerful voice and style to transplant Afro-Cuban music to every corner of the globe. source
  16. In 1997, at a ceremony marking fifty years of her musical career, she gave a stage costume, shoes and all, to the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History. source
  17. In 2024 the United States Mint put her on a quarter as part of its American Women Quarters program. source
  18. If you could never go home again, which song or sound would you carry with you?
Read the transcript of the short and the video
  1. Celia Cruz left Cuba on tour in 1960 and never went back. source
  2. In exile she became the Queen of Salsa, carried Afro-Cuban music around the world, and received the National Medal of Arts from the President. source
  3. She was born in Havana on 21 October 1925, into a poor family. source
  4. According to her biographers, Castro's government barred her from returning to Cuba. source
  5. She made her life in New York and New Jersey, and sang about Cuba for the rest of her career. source
  6. In 1997, at a ceremony marking fifty years of her musical career, she gave a stage costume, shoes and all, to the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History. source
  7. In 2024 the United States Mint put her on a quarter as part of its American Women Quarters program. source
